summary: Describes how Microsoft Internet Explorer and IIS in Windows 2000 use Kerberos, and fall back to NTLM, to secure web transactions. It defines the HTTP authentication scheme named negotiate, which wraps SPNEGO. It documents existing practice and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A browser and a website agree on the safest way to prove who you are, such as a ticket from your company login, and fall back to an older way if needed.

subtitle: Using Kerberos and NTLM for web authentication in Windows with HTTP Negotiate.

tldr.problem: Windows enterprises need strong authentication for web applications but want to use credentials and authentication infrastructure (Kerberos) that users already have from their domain login.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the HTTP auth-scheme called Negotiate, which wraps SPNEGO (Simple and Protected Negotiate mechanism). It allows a browser and web server to negotiate the best authentication method, preferring Kerberos and falling back to NTLM if needed, using the Generic Security Services Application Program Interface (GSSAPI).
tldr.outcome: Microsoft Internet Explorer and Internet Information Services in Windows 2000 can authenticate users for web transactions using the same Kerberos tickets issued by the Windows domain, improving both security and user experience by eliminating separate web passwords.

today: RFC 4559 documents HTTP Negotiate authentication as implemented by Microsoft Windows. While the specification originates from Windows 2000 and IIS, the mechanism has been widely adopted in enterprise environments. Today it remains an important authentication method in Windows-based intranets where Kerberos infrastructure is already deployed, though modern systems increasingly prefer other approaches like OIDC or SAML.

sections.title: Kerberos for Web Authentication
sections.content:
Microsoft Internet Explorer (MSIE) and Internet Information Services (IIS) in Windows 2000 support Kerberos authentication for securing web transactions. This provides enterprises with strong authentication based on the Kerberos v5 protocol, the same security infrastructure that Windows domains already use for user login.

Kerberos authentication on the web is built on previously defined mechanisms: SPNEGO (Simple and Protected GSS-API Negotiation mechanism) as defined in RFC 4178, and the Generic Security Services Application Program Interface (GSSAPI). The HTTP auth-scheme of Negotiate wraps these mechanisms to provide seamless web authentication in Windows environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Windows computers already use a security system called Kerberos when you log in to your company network. Web browsers and servers can now use the same system to verify who you are without needing a separate password.

sections.title: The HTTP Negotiate Scheme
sections.content:
Use of Kerberos for HTTP authentication is wrapped in an HTTP auth-scheme called Negotiate. The auth-params exchanged use data formats defined for use with the GSSAPI. In particular, they follow the formats set for the SPNEGO and Kerberos mechanisms for GSSAPI.

The current implementation is limited to use of SPNEGO with the Kerberos and Microsoft NTLM protocols. When SPNEGO negotiation results in Kerberos, the security services of authentication and, optionally, impersonation are performed. Impersonation means the IIS server assumes the Windows identity of the authenticated principal.
sections.plainLanguage: The Negotiate scheme is like a conversation between the browser and the server. They start by offering Kerberos. If that works, great. If not, they switch to an older backup method called NTLM.

sections.title: Challenge and Response Flow
sections.content:
When a server receives a request for an access-protected object without an acceptable Authorization header, it responds with a 401 Unauthorized status code and a WWW-Authenticate header with the challenge Negotiate (with no gssapi-data in the initial response).

The client obtains user credentials using the SPNEGO GSSAPI mechanism and generates a GSSAPI message to send with a new request including an Authorization header containing base64-encoded data.

The server decodes this data and passes it to the SPNEGO GSSAPI mechanism in the gss_accept_security_context function. If the context is not complete, the server responds with a 401 status code with a WWW-Authenticate header containing the next gssapi-data token.

This challenge-response cycle continues until the security context is complete. When gss_accept_security_context indicates success, the server may supply final authentication data in a 200 response with a WWW-Authenticate header. The client decodes this final data and processes it with gss_init_security_context to confirm successful authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: First, the server says 'prove who you are.' The browser responds with secret information. The server checks it and says 'one more thing.' The browser responds again. Finally, the server says 'OK, I know who you are' and lets you in.

sections.title: Negotiate Operation Example
sections.content:
A client requests a protected document with GET dir/index.html. The server, having no Authorization header, responds with:

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate

The client uses SPNEGO GSSAPI to generate a message and resends with:

GET dir/index.html
Authorization: Negotiate a87421000492aa874209af8bc028

The server decodes the gssapi-data and passes it to SPNEGO GSSAPI. If the context is not complete, the server responds:

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate 749efa7b23409c20b92356

The client decodes this response, processes it with Gss_Init_security_context, and returns new gssapi-data:

GET dir/index.html
Authorization: Negotiate 89a8742aa8729a8b028

This cycle continues until the security context is complete. When successful, the server responds with 200 Success and may include final gssapi-data in a WWW-Authenticate header.
sections.plainLanguage: Browser asks for a page. Server says 'who are you?' Browser sends a code. Server checks it and says 'prove more.' Browser sends more information. Finally server says 'OK, welcome.'

sections.title: Security and Implementation Concerns
sections.content:
The SPNEGO HTTP authentication facility only provides authentication of a user to a server. It does not protect HTTP headers or data, including the Authorization and WWW-Authenticate headers themselves. External security mechanisms such as TLS (Transport Layer Security) must be used to provide confidentiality for the entire HTTP conversation.

Hashes of TLS certificates can be used as channel bindings to secure the authentication channel. Alternatively, Kerb-TLS (RFC 2712) can provide both authentication and confidentiality, though this requires a change to the TLS provider.

This mechanism is not used for HTTP authentication to HTTP proxies. If an HTTP proxy sits between client and server, it must not share authenticated connections between different clients. A proxy that correctly honors client-to-server authentication integrity supplies the Proxy-support: Session-Based-Authentication header. Clients must not use SPNEGO through a proxy unless the proxy supplies this header with the 401 response.

When the client sends user data in PUT or POST requests, the authentication should be complete between client and server before the data is sent. The return status from gss_init_security_context indicates when the security context is complete and the data can be sent safely.
sections.plainLanguage: Negotiate proves who you are, but it does not hide the messages traveling over the network. You need to use TLS encryption to keep eavesdroppers from reading your traffic. Be careful if using an HTTP proxy; it might try to reuse your login for other people.
